value: compromise as a topic of political theory
what the central features of compromise are, and which of its aspects are disputed
a topic-centred review that first clarifies the concept of compromise and then sets out the debated aspects of it

quote: Given the growing literature on compromise, a systematic approach to the topic is due.

But aside from a wide acknowledgment that compromise can constitute a legitimate approach to dealing with disagreement, the literature on compromise is characterized by significant differences and controversies—which is not surprising, given the complexity inherent in the subject of compromise.

value: compromise as a response to disagreement
quote: Like consensus, compromise is a possible response to disagreement or conflict.
None
In its most basic sense, a compromise can be understood as a form of agreement that has the purpose of accommodating conflicting views or claims.
Unlike compromise, consensus requires the parties to a disagreement to change their minds on the controversial issue.
Intersection compromise is based on overlapping principles, while controversial principles are excluded from the agreement.
One option is a conjunction compromise, which integrates some of the conflicting principles ( Lepora, 2012 ; Lepora and Goodin, 2013 ).

Substitution compromise consists only of principles that are not part of the original disagreement ( Lepora, 2012 ; Lepora and Goodin, 2013 )–it “changes the subject,” so to speak ( Weinstock, 2013 : 545).
Moral compromise can be understood to involve principles, that is, beliefs and values that are based on moral convictions and that are often part of one’s identity.
Non-moral compromise, in contrast, pertains to mere interests, including material interests such as income and wealth ( Gutmann and Thompson, 2012 ).
In the interpersonal sense, compromise occurs between different persons who participate in a decision-making process ( May, 2013 ).
In the intrapersonal sense, compromise occurs within a person’s head.
We have pragmatic reasons to compromise if we prefer a specific compromise over the alternative of not compromising regarding the consequences that either option yields.

Margalit argues that “rotten compromises,” that is, agreements to establish inhumane regimes which exert humiliation and cruelty, are never justified—not even for the sake of securing international peace.

Moreover, Mark Warren and Jane Mansbridge (2016) conceive of compromise as a possible outcome of deliberation as well as “deliberative negotiation”, that is, of negotiation processes that are characterized by deliberative features.
However, if we conceive of compromise in a tripolar sense, that is, including third parties that are affected by a compromise, things look differently.
As a militant consociational democracy, the Belgian political system refuses cooperation, including compromise, with extremist parties on both the right and the left.
Moreover, Theodore Benditt points out that moral compromise can negatively affect one’s sense of self.
But even though the parties to a compromise continue disagreeing on a controversial issue, a compromise can prevent their disagreement from spiraling into a full-blown conflict.

It is, for example, conceivable that principled compromisers are more likely to develop trusting relationships with their interlocutors over time, thus achieving perhaps more favorable outcomes for affected third parties in the long run than pragmatic compromisers.

value: The review treats compromise broadly and leaves open what makes a compromise specifically political.
quote: While this survey has addressed compromises broadly conceived—covering compromises between individuals, groups, legislators, and so on—more work is needed on the specifics of compromises in politics, starting with the question of what political compromises are.

value: The role of compromise, as distinct from consensus, in consociational democracies is left unclarified.
quote: However, the precise role of compromise in consociational democracies, and especially its role as distinct from consensus, requires further clarification.

value: Work linking compromise and deliberation is growing, so how to compromise is shifting into deliberative terrain.
quote: Given the mounting work on the connections between compromise and deliberation, it stands to reason that the question of “how to compromise” will increasingly shift into the deliberative terrain.

value: Several theorists hold that no abstract rule can separate acceptable from unacceptable compromises; cases must be judged one by one.
quote: Margalit (2010) similarly urges a case-by-case evaluation of the merit of concrete compromises, emphasizing that abstract rules cannot cover all possible scenarios in which a normative evaluation of compromise is necessary.

value: The literature agrees that a compromise consists of mutual and voluntary concessions.
quote: An undisputed feature of compromise is that it consists of mutual and voluntary concessions ( Bellamy et al., 2012 ; Bohman, 1996 ; Jones and O’Flynn, 2012 ; Lepora, 2012 ; Lepora and Goodin, 2013 ; Margalit, 2010 ; May, 2013 ).

value: arguments for principled compromise that May rejects
quote: By way of rejecting four arguments in favor of principled compromise (complexity, respect, accommodation, and reciprocity), May argues that moral compromises cannot be justified for other than pragmatic reasons, especially given the fact that moral compromises inevitably involve a moral loss for the compromising person.
